newsitem.title: HAITI: Five dead in gang violence in Haitian slum.
newsitem.headline: Five dead in gang violence in Haitian slum.

text.p: Up to five people were killed and several houses set ablaze overnight in worsening gang warfare in the Port-au-Prince slum of Cite Soleil, witnesses and local media said on Wednesday.
U.N. peacekeeping troops and foreign and Haitian police arrived on the scene on Wednesday morning to remove corpses and secure the area so firefighters could put out the fires.
"It is very dangerous here right now," Police Trainer Christine Girard said at the border of two warring neighbourhoods, Pele and Cite Boston.
Girard said four bodies were found and local radio reported five people were killed.
Gang violence has escalated over recent weeks in Cite Soleil, home to 200,000 of Haiti's poorest people, with the death toll standing at more than 10 with the latest bloodshed.
Most shops and businesses remained shuttered, and many people stayed off the streets.

Some Cite Soleil residents blamed the violence on the desperate economic situation in the area, where most people are without jobs and many going hungry. Others blamed drug-trafficking, turf wars and too much alcohol as the cause for the constant gunfire.
"If people don't have money to buy food how are there so many guns," asked one bystander, James Pierrot.
Cite Soleil Police Chief Johnny Esterville was shot at on Tuesday morning.

Gang members on all sides claimed to be protecting their neighbourhood from others. Hoodlums can be seen roaming the streets armed with weapons ranging from pistols to automiatic weapons -- sometimes with a gun in each hand.
"The gangs are armed with all kinds of guns and we have not yet determined where they got them," said Delmas Police Commissioner Guy Phillipe, who has jurisdiction over the area.
Cite Soleil residents said they saw street children steal guns from U.S. troops during the intervention which restored former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power in 1994.

"The trucks went by and the street kids jumped up on them and stole a lot of guns," said a Cite Boston resident. "Since then, the guns have been stored under the ground or in little shelters in pillowcases."

Sources at the U.S. embassy and the U.S. Support Group mission in Haiti both denied knowledge of stolen weapons. But one U.S. Army source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said a huge weapons cache, including as many as 180 M-16s, was stolen in the Cite Soleil area.
The weapons were being transported without the firing clips necessary to use them, he added.
